coverage.why: fnv-1a-hash plus deterministic-seeding names the same deterministic-hash-to-distribute idea, while answer-position-randomization is the mechanism, not the assessment-validity concern that position bias names, and modulo-bias is about uneven residues rather than bias in assessment.
rate-limiting-cooldown-window and key-value-state-table name the same throttling and KV-rows-in-SQL ideas, while nothing logged expresses ordering checks cheapest-first.

sqlite-wal-mode is wal-journal-mode and idempotent-retry-safety is idempotency-and-safe-retries, but no logged concept names the busy-timeout-versus-retry tradeoff — the two mechanisms are logged separately, never their comparison.

verdicts.why: The hash function is a literal FNV-1a implementation — offset basis 2166136261, prime 16777619, xor-then-multiply per byte, with Math.imul for 32-bit wraparound — so reading it teaches the actual algorithm.
The code derives an answer slot from a hash of the question text so the same input always yields the same position, which is exactly what deterministic seeding means and shows why a PRNG was avoided.

The code hits modulo bias (`hash % 4` over a 2^32 range is fine here since 4 divides evenly, so no bias exists) but nothing in it names, demonstrates, or corrects the phenomenon — a reader learns FNV-1a hashing, not modulo bias.
`h >>> 0` is the load-bearing line that converts the signed 32-bit result of Math.imul into an unsigned integer, and dropping it would make the modulo yield negative slots — real, learnable use.
Math.imul is used precisely for its wrapping 32-bit signed multiply in the FNV-1a step, and the >>> 0 to get back to unsigned shows why it's needed over plain `*`.

The code is exactly a deterministic answer-slot placement derived from hashing the question seed, so a reader learns the mechanism — and that it is deterministic, not random, which is the interesting part of the concept.
Every guard path returns 0 and the handler never throws, so the code demonstrably shows a hook that fails open by exiting zero on missing db, missing session, or disabled config.
Code implements a real cooldown window plus grace period and max-attempt cap over persisted timestamps, so a reader learns the actual mechanics of rate-limiting a nudge.
The code stores structured session state as a delimited string in a generic meta key/value table, showing the namespaced key, encode/decode pair, and pruning that define the pattern.
Code packs three fields into one pipe-joined meta value and splits it back with fallbacks for empty/NaN parts — a real, readable instance of delimited-string serialization.

GRACE_MINUTES gates the first nudge behind minutesSince(state.first), with the first sighting only recording state and returning — a readable instance of deferring a side effect until a thing has persisted long enough.

The `if (input.agent_id) return 0;` line skips subagent sessions, but it is one unexplained guard clause with no subagent context, delegation model, or invocation mechanics visible — the code is about nudge state machines and cooldowns, not subagent invocation.
Code writes a single JSON line with hookSpecificOutput to stdout and returns exit 0, showing the hook's stdout-JSON contract in real use, though the payload body is elided.

It sets journal_mode=WAL alongside busy_timeout and a busy-retry loop, so the reader learns both how WAL is turned on and the writer-contention/SQLITE_BUSY behaviour that makes retrying safe under it.
The code both sets `busy_timeout = 5000` and wraps calls in a SQLITE_BUSY retry loop, showing what the pragma does and why an application-level retry is still needed after it expires.

The loop shows the core pattern — bounded attempts, retry only on a transient (busy) error, rethrow everything else, escalating sleep per attempt index — so a reader learns real retry-with-backoff mechanics, even though the delay curve hides inside sleepBriefly.
No transaction is begun, committed, or rolled back here — the rollback claim lives only in a comment justifying the retry; the code actually exercises SQLITE_BUSY retry and WAL pragmas.

The retry loop plus its comment turn on exactly why re-running the operation is safe — the busy transaction already rolled back, so the write leaves no partial effect — which is the core of retry safety.
The catch block inspects the error with isBusy and rethrows anything it doesn't own, which is the whole point of discriminating errors in a catch rather than swallowing them.

The FK pragma is one toggle line with no constraints, cascades, or violation handling in sight — the code's real subject is SQLITE_BUSY retry, so a reader learns nothing about how foreign key enforcement behaves.
